title: A Revolut revolution, or just another big bank?
full_text:
A dry two-sentence statement from the financial regulator was enough to rattle the biggest banks in the land.
Three years in the making, APRA’s decision to give the green light to London-headquartered Revolut to become a bank here is shaping as the biggest threat to the nation’s banks since – well – the last disrupter made a play.
There’s no question the big banks have stared down “banking lite” challengers before. Names such as Xinja and Volt have come and gone. Digital-only ME Bank has long been swallowed up, and even business-focused Judo is now facing its own substantial growing pains.
No doubt, Revolut’s entry will be a much bigger fight for the big four. Its slick banking app and proprietary tech is proven, and it offers global payments reach far advanced of what they have in their toolkit. However, the degree of success this time depends on whether the big four see themselves as defenders or disrupters alongside Revolut.
And while Revolut’s mobile-based payments platform has plenty of momentum behind it, the European tech champion’s own challenge is that Macquarie Bank – with its clean product offering and generous pricing – is years ahead as a digital first-mover.
It was the disruptive force of Macquarie that allowed it to cherrypick the big banks’ wealthiest customers, quickly capturing between 6 per cent and 7 per cent of both the home loan and deposit market.
However, Macquarie’s actions have also forced the big four to become digitally match fit, with each lender having spent up big overhauling their respective banking apps and deposits offerings in the past five years.
Commonwealth Bank leads the pack with seamless share trading and banking features. ANZ was late to the party but went in with ambition, spending more than $1bn – though it is still in the process of rolling out the much-hyped overhaul to customers. Macquarie hasn’t disclosed its investment in its digital banking platform over recent years, but some rivals estimate it has pushed $1bn.
ANZ has made noises about following Macquarie’s lead and paying up for “lazy deposits” that disproportionately sit on Commonwealth Bank’s and Westpac’s balance sheets.
This no doubt will spark a pricing war to crush all comers, as well as profits. But given Macquarie has already secured the best of all the banks’ retail customers, those likely left over will be less savings-rich and therefore the cost of chasing the rest of the bunch seems too high.
Those most vulnerable to Revolut’s local banking franchise include Bendigo Bank, whose digital-only Up Bank – with more than one million accounts – competes squarely for the same under-35 demographic that Revolut is targeting. Bank of Queensland will also feel the pinch, while AMP is looking to reboot its digital-only bank amid persistent talk of a sale.
At the same time, HSBC is poised to sell its Australian retail bank, a move that could put more customers up for grabs.
Calling Revolut a neo-bank or start-up probably understates its mass. The privately held lender’s latest funding round gave it a valuation of $US75bn ($107bn), placing it just behind ANZ. It is targeting a stockmarket listing – probably in London – in the coming years. The fast-growing bank has more than 75 million retail customers globally, is profitable ($3.25bn last year in Australian dollar terms) and deposits are running at just under $100bn globally.
But significantly, the nature of those deposits is small, which suggests it needs to run much harder and tighter to maintain reasonable returns. The average balance is about $1300, meaning all those transactions come at a far greater cost. CBA’s average deposits, by comparison, is $36,000 across its 12 million customers.
As The Australian’s Max Atchinson revealed, Revolut enlisted former ANZ chief and one-time Westpac chairman John McFarlane as an adviser to help smooth the way for its banking licence. But there’s a broader ANZ contingent behind it. Revolut Australia’s directors include a former ANZ senior executive during the McFarlane era, Rob Gouwaard (who serves as Revolut’s local chair). Also on the local board is former GE Money Australia boss and one-time ANZ chief risk officer Mike Cutter. Rounding out the board is Dee McGrath, a one-time NAB executive and current ASX director. Revolut local chief executive is former Virgin Money and Bank of Queensland retail boss Matt Baxby.
Revolut has been operating in Australia since 2019 under Baxby and already has more than 1.2 million customers, offering share trading, payments, forex, international transfers and crypto.
Baxby’s key contention is that with deposits now secured and plans to scale up into lending products, Revolut is able to offer an integration of banking services that no bank has brought to the Australian market before. And unlike Macquarie, it is also going after business customers.
The aim is to “build the most seamless, secure and customer-first banking experience for Australian consumers and businesses,” he says.
The challenger has some unlikely champions. JPMorgan boss Jamie Dimon called out the likes of Revolut – along with other fintechs Stripe and Jack Dorsey’s Block – in this year’s annual letter to investors as “successful examples” of challengers able to outmanoeuvre slow-moving incumbents often weighed down by complexity, bureaucracy and complacency.
“Being a company of sizeable magnitude makes it easier to ignore new competitors since they often start small in one product but move rapidly to expand,” wrote Dimon, whose bank is the biggest in the US.
Revolut opened for business on day one of getting its local licence, this week offering 3 per cent interest on savings and transaction accounts up to $1m. (Macquarie is offering up to 5 per cent on up to $2m.) Revolut has also launched a local version of its popular fee-free credit card.
Revolut’s Australian application moved faster than its home market, where it waited five years to receive its UK banking licence – this was finally approved in March.
Last month, Revolut’s UK-based parent injected $85m into the local unit to seed the Australian bank, and Baxby says there’s plans to invest $400m over the next few years. It already employs more than 120 people locally, with staff numbers expected to increase as it adds products.
Even so, sometimes it will be a case of careful what you wish for. Being a bank in Australia gives you depositor protection (up to $250,000) but is an expensive exercise with scale needed to ease the high-cost regulation. Revolut’s cross-border payments and crypto edge (held separately from the deposits) will also come under close scrutiny from white collar crimes regulator Austrac.
Ireland is held up as an example of the damage Revolut can inflict on incumbents. There, it has managed to secure a staggering one in two retail bank customers. It also dominates accounts in Italy. Its edge has been fast payments – in fact, it has become a verb, with the Irish easily saying “I’ll Rev it to you” to describe a funds transfer.
Still, those same customers aren’t quite ready to cut the cord, with Revolut usually remaining a customer’s second bank account across Europe. Big transactions and loans still come through big banks.
As technology lowered barriers to entry, Europe has offered just the right conditions for a player like Revolut to grow. The market has a myriad of cross-border payments (inside and outside the EU), its banks are notoriously slow-moving and defensive, and many are still traumatised by the GFC.
It’s a different market here. The banks are well capitalised, and Australians, while they love to travel, do most of their banking at home. Australians are also notoriously sticky – this inertia has fuelled the profits of the big four.
Macquarie the challenger isn’t taking the Revolut threat lying down. It sensed something was in the wind and this month it lifted its savings game with a new high-interest digital term deposit account – 5.2 per cent for 12 months – that allows for early withdrawal without penalties. Macquarie has been building its digital bank for more than a decade longer than Revolut, but isn’t prepared to give up its crown as the banking disruption king. johnstone@theaustralian. com.au
